Nojima H.lab_name: Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University (Kobe, Japan)
Nojima H.role: First author of the 2003 Kobe study showing that raptor grabs mTOR's targets through a short TOS motif, the docking step that lets mTORC1 reach its substrates
Nojima H.sub: Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University, Kazuyoshi Yonezawa group (at the time of the study, 2003)
story: An enzyme like mTOR has to find the right proteins to act on. In 2002 two groups discovered raptor, a partner protein that sits next to mTOR in the complex now called mTORC1, the growth-control complex. One of those groups was Kazuyoshi Yonezawa's team at Kobe University. Hiroki Nojima was first author of their 2003 follow-up in the Journal of Biological Chemistry (NOJ2003).

The study showed that raptor binds two of mTOR's best-known targets, p70 S6 kinase and 4E-BP1, both of which control how fast cells make proteins. Raptor holds them through a short stretch of five amino acids called the TOS motif (TOR signalling motif). When the motif was changed, raptor could no longer bind and mTOR could no longer act on the target. This made raptor the part of mTORC1 that presents substrates to the kinase, a model that has held up in later structural work. The experiments were done in cultured cells and with purified proteins.
PubMed lists Nojima at the Biosignal Research Center of Kobe University. No other paper could be tied to this person with confidence, so later career steps are not known.

highlights.NOJ2003: First author: showed that raptor binds S6 kinase and 4E-BP1 through their TOS motifs, which lets mTORC1 present these substrates to the kinase.

Nojima H.note: Other PubMed records under 'Nojima H' belong to Hideaki Nojima (zebrafish, Osaka) and Hiroshi Nojima (Osaka); not used.

Hidayat S.lab_name: Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University (Kobe, Japan)
Hidayat S.role: Member of Kazuyoshi Yonezawa's Kobe team that co-discovered raptor and worked out how mTOR senses amino acids, and first author of a study showing that a leucine derivative can block amino acid-mTOR signalling
Hidayat S.sub: Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University, Kazuyoshi Yonezawa group (PubMed records 2000–2006, at the time of the studies)
story: In 2002 two teams, one in Boston and one in Kobe, reported raptor, the partner protein that defines mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Sujuti Hidayat is a co-author of the Kobe paper in Cell (HARA2002). It showed that raptor is needed for mTOR to act on 4E-BP1 and S6 kinase, two proteins that control protein synthesis, and that silencing raptor in the worm C. elegans mimics loss of TOR. Hidayat is also a co-author of the 2003 follow-up (NOJ2003) showing that raptor holds these targets through a short TOS motif.

Hidayat's own first-author paper from the same group, published in 2003, tested a chemical cousin of the amino acid leucine. It blocked the amino acid signal to mTOR in human Jurkat cells, a line of immune cells, and stopped them in the G1 phase of the cell cycle. That study lists Hidayat at the Biosignal Research Center of Kobe University.

PubMed records place Hidayat in the Yonezawa group from 2000 to 2006, on papers about the tail region of mTOR that the enzyme needs to work (2000), about how the Hsp90 inhibitor geldanamycin disrupts the mTOR-raptor pathway (2006), and about the two motifs of 4E-BP1 that bind raptor (2006). A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.HARA2002: Co-author: part of the Kobe team that co-discovered raptor and showed it is needed for mTOR to act on 4E-BP1 and S6 kinase.
highlights.NOJ2003: Co-author: contributed to the study showing that raptor binds mTOR substrates through their TOS motif.

Hidayat S.note: Previous profile used 'him'; pronoun removed because no source states it. Tokunaga C.lab_name: Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University (Kobe, Japan)
Tokunaga C.role: Member of Kazuyoshi Yonezawa's Kobe team that co-discovered raptor, and first author of a 2004 review on how mTOR combines amino acid and energy signals
Tokunaga C.sub: Biosignal Research Center, Kobe University, Kazuyoshi Yonezawa group (PubMed records 2000–2006, at the time of the studies)
story: Chiharu Tokunaga is a co-author of the 2002 Cell paper from Kobe University (HARA2002) that, together with a Boston study in the same issue, reported raptor, the partner protein that defines mTORC1, the growth-control complex. The Kobe team showed that raptor is needed for mTOR to act on 4E-BP1 and S6 kinase and that silencing raptor in worms mimics loss of TOR. Tokunaga is also a co-author of the 2003 follow-up (NOJ2003), which found that raptor holds these two targets through a short TOS motif and so presents them to the kinase.

In 2004 Tokunaga was first author, with Ken-ichi Yoshino and Kazuyoshi Yonezawa, of a review in Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications explaining how mTOR brings together two kinds of information, whether amino acids are available and whether the cell has enough energy. PubMed lists Tokunaga at the Biosignal Research Center of Kobe University on that review.

Other PubMed records from the same group, from 2000 to 2006, include work on the tail region of mTOR that the enzyme needs to work, on a leucine derivative that blocks amino acid signalling to mTOR, on how the Hsp90 inhibitor geldanamycin disrupts the mTOR-raptor pathway, and on the motifs of 4E-BP1 that bind raptor. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.HARA2002: Co-author: part of the Kobe team that co-discovered raptor and showed it is needed for mTOR to act on 4E-BP1 and S6 kinase.
highlights.NOJ2003: Co-author: contributed to the study showing that raptor binds mTOR substrates through their TOS motif.

Tokunaga C.note: A 2026 paper by 'Chiho Tokunaga' (Tsukuba cardiovascular surgery) is a different person and was not used.

Imseng S.lab_name: Maier Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Imseng S.role: Structural biologist from Timm Maier's group at the Biozentrum Basel who helped solve the first detailed structures of human mTORC1 and mTORC2 and then worked on a drug to block mTORC1 specifically
Imseng S.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel (PubMed affiliation 2013–2021, at the time of the studies) · PhD, University of Basel (2016, thesis on the structure of mTORC1, advisors Timm Maier and Tilman Schirmer)
story: To see how a protein machine works, structural biologists try to see its shape. Stefan Imseng is a co-author of three Atlas studies that did this for the two mTOR complexes using cryo-electron microscopy, which photographs frozen protein molecules and combines thousands of images into a 3D model. The 2015 Science paper (AYL2015) showed the architecture of human mTORC1, the growth-control complex: two copies of mTOR and its partners form a diamond-shaped dimer, and the structure showed how rapamycin bound to its helper protein FKBP12 narrows the entrance to the active site. The 2018 eLife paper (STU2018) did the same for the core of mTORC2, and the 2020 Science Advances paper (SCA2020) sharpened that picture to 3.2 angstroms, showing that the end of the partner protein Rictor covers the spot where rapamycin would bind. That explains why mTORC2 resists rapamycin.

Imseng did doctoral work in Timm Maier's structural biology group at the Biozentrum. The 2016 thesis, supervised by Maier and Tilman Schirmer, was titled 'Structural studies on the target of rapamycin complex 1'. Imseng was first author of a 2018 review on the architecture and activation of the PI3K-related kinase family to which mTOR belongs, and a co-author of later Basel studies on how DEPTOR regulates both mTOR complexes (2021) and on how mTORC1 recognises its substrate 4E-BP1 (2021).

In 2018 the Biozentrum announced an Innosuisse-funded project in which Imseng and Asier Gonzalez, supported by Timm Maier and Michael Hall, set out to develop a lead compound that blocks mTORC1 specifically, as a possible drug for tuberous sclerosis. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.AYL2015: Co-author: part of the team that solved the cryo-EM architecture of human mTORC1, including its complex with FKBP12-rapamycin.
highlights.STU2018: Co-author: contributed to the first architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex.
highlights.SCA2020: Co-author: contributed to the 3.2 angstrom structure of human mTORC2 that pinpoints Rictor as the cause of its rapamycin insensitivity.

Imseng S.note: The Biozentrum news page uses 'his'; text avoids pronouns. Outcome of the 2018-2020 Innosuisse spin-off project not known.

Sauer E.role: Structural biologist at the Biozentrum Basel who worked on the structure of the mTOR kinase and contributed to the cryo-EM structures of human mTORC1 and mTORC2
Sauer E.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel (PubMed affiliation 2013–2018, at the time of the studies)
story: Evelyn Sauer is a co-author of two Atlas studies from Basel that used cryo-electron microscopy to show the shape of the mTOR complexes. The 2015 Science paper (AYL2015) gave the first detailed architecture of human mTORC1, the growth-control complex, including how rapamycin bound to its helper protein FKBP12 narrows access to the active site. The 2018 eLife paper (STU2018) did the same for the core of mTORC2, made of mTOR, Rictor, SIN1 and mLST8, and helped explain why mTORC2 resists rapamycin.

Sauer was first author, with Stefan Imseng, Timm Maier and Michael Hall, of a 2013 review in Biochemical Society Transactions on the conserved sequence motifs and structure of the mTOR kinase domain, the part of the enzyme that transfers phosphate groups. Earlier Basel work by Sauer was in protein crystallography: a 2013 single-author paper on the structure and RNA binding of the bacterial protein Hfq, and a 2014 study of the cell-death regulator BCL-W solved with designed binding proteins.
PubMed lists Sauer at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel on all of these papers. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.AYL2015: Co-author: contributed to the cryo-EM architecture of human mTORC1.
highlights.STU2018: Co-author: contributed to the architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex.

Sauer E.note: No official page found. Ancient-DNA papers by 'Eberhard Sauer' (Edinburgh) are a different person.

Battaglioni S.lab_name: Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Battaglioni S.role: Cell biologist in Michael Hall's group at the Biozentrum Basel, first author of a 2022 Cell review that catalogued the direct substrates of mTOR
Battaglioni S.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall group (PubMed affiliation 2020–2024) · Institute of Biochemistry, ETH Zurich (PubMed affiliation 2020)
story: mTOR is a kinase, an enzyme that switches other proteins on or off by attaching phosphate groups to them. Which proteins it acts on decides what mTOR does in the cell. Stefania Battaglioni is first author of the 2022 Cell review in this Atlas (BAT2022), written with Michael Hall, which gathered the known direct substrates of mTOR and explained how the two complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, end up acting on different targets. It is a reference map for anyone trying to trace a signal from mTOR to an effect.

Battaglioni's own lab work in the Hall group looks for new mTOR substrates. A 2024 PNAS paper, with Battaglioni as first author, showed that mTORC1 phosphorylates and stabilises a protein called LST2, which in turn holds back the EGF receptor, a growth-factor receptor. A 2023 EMBO Journal study, on which Battaglioni is a co-author, found that yeast TORC1 switches off Stm1, a factor that keeps ribosomes dormant, so that protein synthesis can restart when nutrients return.

Battaglioni also contributed to a 2020 Nature Metabolism study, led from ETH Zurich, showing that the pH inside cells helps drive cell division and tumour growth by raising cyclin D1. PubMed lists Battaglioni at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel through 2024. A current job title could not be confirmed.

highlights.BAT2022: First author: wrote, with Michael Hall, the Cell review that catalogues direct mTOR substrates and how mTORC1 and mTORC2 choose their targets.

Battaglioni S.note: No official profile page found; position from PubMed only.
